claims.claim: The working definition of debt: Investor.gov's glossary defines debt as an amount owed to a person or organization for borrowed funds, and states that loans, notes, bonds, and mortgages are forms of debt that all call for borrowers to pay back the amount they owe, typically with interest, by a specific date set forth in the repayment terms. Investopedia agrees: debt is something, usually money, owed by one party to another, which must be paid back, typically with added interest, unless forgiven by the lender.

Interest is the price paid for borrowing money, expressed as a percentage rate over a period of time (Investor.gov glossary 'Interest'); from the borrower's side, a company's cost of debt is the interest rate it would have to pay (OpenStax 17.2); interest compensates the lender for taking on the risk of the loan (Investopedia).

There are two broad types of capital: debt (or borrowing) and equity (or ownership); companies typically finance their assets through equity, selling ownership shares to stockholders, and through debt, borrowing money from lenders; the debt that a firm uses is often referred to as financial leverage (OpenStax 17.1).

The most common forms of debt are loans (mortgages, auto loans, personal loans), in which the borrower receives a set amount of money and must repay it in full, with interest, by a certain date; credit cards and lines of credit are revolving or open-end credit, with no fixed end date, where the borrower is assigned a credit limit and can use, repay, and reuse the credit (Investopedia); bonds are a debt security, similar to an IOU, in which the issuer promises to pay interest during the life of the bond and to repay the principal, the face value, when it matures (Investor.gov glossary 'Bonds').
Principal is the total amount of money being borrowed or lent; the initial amount of money invested (Investor.gov glossary 'Principal').

Debt carries obligations: a repayment schedule (borrowers must pay back the amount owed by a specific date set forth in the repayment terms; Investopedia's student-loan example describes fixed monthly payments until the debt is paid off), interest payments during the life of the debt (Investor.gov glossary 'Bonds'), and seniority, in which a senior bond has a higher priority than another bond's claim to the same class of assets in case of default or bankruptcy (Investor.gov glossary 'Senior Bond'); default is a failure to pay principal or interest when due (Investor.gov glossary 'Default').

Why businesses borrow: debt is used to make large purchases that could not be afforded otherwise, and for companies, access to debt can make all the difference in their ability to expand and compete (Investopedia); debt is one of the two broad sources of capital financing a company's assets (OpenStax 17.1).

Leverage risks: companies that take on a large amount of debt may not be able to make their interest payments if sales drop, putting the business in danger of bankruptcy; even short of that, too much debt can impose a crippling burden, requiring a company to devote much of its income to debt repayment rather than more productive purposes (Investopedia).

The honest framing: debt is a tool with a schedule. Every form of debt calls for the borrower to pay back the amount owed, typically with interest, by a specific date set in the repayment terms, and the payments are contractual obligations that do not bend with the borrower's fortunes (Investor.gov glossary 'Liability/Debt'; Investopedia).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources frame the scope of debt slightly differently: Investor.gov's glossary defines debt narrowly as amounts owed for borrowed funds, while Investopedia defines debt broadly as anything, usually money, owed by one party to another.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the borrowed-funds framing as the working definition (matching the finance meaning used throughout the lesson), while Investopedia's broader framing supports the core idea that debt must be repaid, typically with interest.
